title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
abstract: While large language models can perform reasoning and acting separately, combining them remains challenging. We propose ReAct, a framework that interleaves verbal reasoning traces and task-specific actions in a single loop. Experiments show that ReAct outperforms acting-only and reasoning-only baselines on question answering, fact verification, and interactive decision making, while producing more interpretable trajectories. A limitation is that the approach depends on the quality of the surrounding tool interfaces.

title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
abstract: Language models struggle with basic factual knowledge and arithmetic. We propose Toolformer, a model trained to decide which APIs to call, when to call them, and how to incorporate the results. Experiments show that Toolformer achieves substantially improved zero-shot performance across many downstream tasks without sacrificing core language modeling ability. However the self-supervised annotation process requires a seed model with reliable in-context learning.

title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Language agents often repeat the same mistakes across trials. We introduce Reflexion, a framework that converts environment feedback into verbal self-reflections stored in episodic memory. Experiments show that Reflexion improves success rates on decision making, coding, and reasoning benchmarks without updating model weights. A limitation is that reflection quality degrades when feedback is sparse or delayed.

title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
abstract: Building complex LLM applications requires composing multiple models, tools, and human inputs. We propose AutoGen, an open-source framework that models workflows as conversations among customizable agents. Experiments show that AutoGen supports diverse applications such as code generation, math problem solving, and automated trading with strong performance. A limitation is that conversation-based orchestration makes cost and termination behavior harder to predict.

title: MetaGPT: Meta Programming for A Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework
abstract: Multi-agent systems built on LLMs often fail to coordinate on complex software tasks. We introduce MetaGPT, which encodes human standard operating procedures into role specifications and structured artifacts. Experiments show that MetaGPT generates more coherent software solutions than conversational multi-agent baselines. However the framework relies on carefully authored role prompts, which limits transfer to open-ended domains.

title: Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
abstract: Open-ended embodied agents require continual exploration and skill acquisition. We present Voyager, an agent that uses an automatic curriculum, a skill library, and iterative prompting to explore Minecraft without human intervention. Results show that Voyager obtains significantly more unique items and unlocks tech tree milestones faster than prior agents. A limitation is that the skill library must be manually inspected for unsafe behaviors.

title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
abstract: Existing benchmarks evaluate language models as chatbots rather than as agents. We propose AgentBench, a multi-dimensional benchmark covering operating systems, databases, knowledge graphs, and web environments. Experiments show that commercial models still struggle with long-horizon reasoning and that open-source models lag far behind. A limitation is that environment instability can introduce evaluation noise.

title: WebArena: A Realistic Web Environment for Building Autonomous Agents
abstract: Most web agent evaluations rely on simplified sandboxes. We introduce WebArena, a realistic, reproducible environment with fully functional websites across e-commerce, forums, and content management. Experiments show that the best GPT-4 agent solves only a small fraction of tasks, far below human performance. However the environment requires substantial engineering effort to host and maintain.

title: ToolLLM: Facilitating Large Language Models to Master 16000+ Real-world APIs
abstract: Open-source models remain weak at calling large collections of real APIs. We present ToolLLM, a data construction and training framework built on a depth-first search decision tree over 16000+ APIs. Experiments show that the trained model generalizes to unseen APIs and outperforms prior open-source tool-use models. A limitation is that the constructed instructions may not reflect production latency constraints.

title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
abstract: Simulating believable human behavior requires memory, planning, and reflection over long horizons. We propose generative agents that store observations in a memory stream and retrieve them by relevance, recency, and importance. Experiments show that the agents produce coherent social behaviors in a small town simulation. However the evaluation is largely qualitative and does not scale to large populations.

title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
abstract: Retrieval-augmented models often retrieve indiscriminately and cannot judge whether evidence is useful. We introduce Self-RAG, which trains a model to emit reflection tokens that decide when to retrieve and how to critique generations. Results show improved factual accuracy and citation quality across open-domain QA tasks. A limitation is the additional inference cost of reflection and retrieval steps.

title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
abstract: Fixed context windows prevent language models from maintaining long conversations and large document state. We present MemGPT, which manages a tiered memory hierarchy and uses function calls to move information between context and external storage. Experiments show improved performance on long-document analysis and multi-session dialogue. However the paging policy adds latency and can evict information that later becomes relevant.

title: AgentTuning: Enabling Generalized Agent Abilities for LLMs
abstract: Aligned language models still lack robust agent capabilities. We introduce AgentTuning, a lightweight instruction-tuning strategy using a collected agent trajectory dataset. Experiments show that AgentTuning improves agent task success while preserving general language abilities. A limitation is that gains diminish when the target environment differs substantially from the tuning distribution.

title: Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agents
abstract: Human evaluation of agent trajectories is expensive and inconsistent. We propose Agent-as-a-Judge, which uses agentic evaluators to inspect intermediate steps rather than only final outputs. Experiments show high agreement with human judgments at a fraction of the cost across coding and web tasks. However evaluator bias can propagate when the judge shares the same failure modes as the evaluated agent.

title: OSWorld: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Open-Ended Tasks in Real Computer Environments
abstract: Multimodal agents are increasingly expected to operate real computers. We introduce OSWorld, a scalable environment with real operating system applications and execution-based evaluation. Experiments show that agents perform far below humans on multi-step tasks, especially when they must recover from errors. A limitation is that environment variability can make results difficult to reproduce exactly.

title: Magentic-One: A Generalist Multi-Agent System for Solving Complex Tasks
abstract: Generalist agents must coordinate specialized capabilities across open-ended tasks. We present Magentic-One, a multi-agent system with an orchestrator that maintains a task ledger and delegates to web, file, and coding agents. Experiments show competitive results on benchmarks spanning browsing, information gathering, and code execution. However orchestration overhead grows quickly with task length and the number of specialists.
